title: The TCP Maximum Segment Size and Related Topics
summary: This RFC clarifies the TCP Maximum Segment Size option and how it interacts with IP, offering advice to implementers. It explains what the option means and why getting it wrong causes trouble. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 7805 and RFC 9293.

plainLanguage.summary: When you mail a package you need to know the biggest box the post office takes. This note explains how two computers tell each other the biggest chunk of data they will accept.

questions: what is tcp maximum segment size
how does the tcp mss option work
what is the default tcp mss
how is mss calculated from mtu
subtitle: The memo that pins down what the TCP Maximum Segment Size option counts: the IP datagram size minus forty.

tldr.problem: The TCP Maximum Segment Size option was ambiguous, because the IP and TCP headers can both vary in length, so implementers disagreed about what number to announce.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 879 sets one rule: the TCP maximum segment size is the IP maximum datagram size minus forty. The default datagram size is 576, so the default segment size is 536.
tldr.outcome: RFC 879 is now Historic. It was obsoleted by RFC 7805 and RFC 9293 and updated by RFC 6691.

today: RFC 879 is Historic. It was obsoleted by RFC 7805 and RFC 9293, and it was updated by RFC 6691, so read those for the current guidance.

sections.title: Why the MSS Needed Clarifying
sections.content:
This memo is a clarification of the TCP specification and is described as containing advice to implementers. The TCP Maximum Segment Size (MSS) option was ambiguous, partly because the IP and TCP headers have variable size, and some implementations had made assumptions about non-default datagram sizes with unfortunate results.

It restates a long-established rule: hosts MUST NOT send datagrams larger than 576 octets unless they have specific knowledge that the destination is prepared to accept larger ones. To fix the ambiguity it adds a new rule: the TCP maximum segment size is the IP maximum datagram size minus forty. With the default datagram size of 576, the default MSS is 536.
sections.plainLanguage: Two computers kept guessing different answers to how big a chunk is allowed to be. This note picks one clear rule so everybody counts the same way.

sections.title: The MSS Option and Datagram Sizes
sections.content:
Every host is required to accept or reassemble datagrams up to 576 octets, and its reassembly buffer must be at least that big. Hosts may accept larger datagrams, but they must not send them without knowing the destination can take them.

The MSS option is sent only when a connection is established. It goes from the data receiver to the data sender and says that the receiver can accept TCP segments up to size X. The RFC notes that it is often mistakenly called a negotiation: it is an announcement. It works independently in each direction, so the two directions can end up with quite different maximum sizes.

The MSS counts only data octets. It does not count the TCP header or the IP header. The correspondence between TCP segments and IP datagrams must be one to one, because TCP expects exactly one complete segment in each block of data IP hands up.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer says once, when it first says hello, the biggest piece of mail it can open. Each side can say a different size, and only the stuff inside the envelope is counted, not the envelope.

sections.title: Three Ways to Count Headers
sections.content:
The calculation is MSS = MTU - sizeof(TCPHDR) - sizeof(IPHDR), where MTU is the maximum packet size on the directly attached network. A sender works out its limit as SndMaxSegSiz = MIN((MTU - sizeof(TCPHDR) - sizeof(IPHDR)), MSS). The question is what header sizes to assume, and the RFC lists three positions.

The conservative position assumes both headers are 60 octets, the moderate one assumes a 60-octet IP header and a 20-octet TCP header, and the liberal one assumes 20 octets for each. The RFC settles on the liberal one, partly because with no MSS option a sender may fill a 576-octet datagram with minimum headers, giving 536 data octets, and the rule should match that default. It also points out that most datagrams use minimum headers, so the other choices waste space: 536/576 is 93% data, 496/576 is 86% and 456/576 is 79%.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine the envelope has a stamp box that could be small or big. The note decides to assume the small one, because that is what most letters really use.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Layer Cooperation
sections.content:
A source host would not normally create fragments. Fragments usually arise when a gateway must send a datagram into a network with a smaller maximum packet size, and gateways must be prepared to fragment. A source may fragment when the receiver announced a large MSS (the RFC's example is 5000 octets) that is larger than its own network allows, but the fragments must not combine to more than the destination accepts. A source that sends large datagrams without knowing the destination can take them, and expects the gateway to cut them down to default size, is called misguided and outlawed.

TCP and IP are distinct layers, and IP keeps no memory of earlier datagrams, so it should not track per-host size limits. Instead the RFC describes careful communication between modules: IP asks the network driver for the MTU, TCP asks IP for the Maximum Datagram Data Size (the MTU minus the IP header length), and TCP can announce an MSS equal to that value minus the TCP header length.

As a footnote it lists some MTUs: ARPANET and MILNET 1007, 10Mb Ethernet 1500 and Proteon PRONET 2046.
sections.plainLanguage: The post office can chop a big parcel into smaller ones, but you should only send a big parcel when you know the receiver can handle it. The two parts of the computer have to talk to each other about sizes.

sections.title: The Default MSS and Its Consequences
sections.content:
The default MSS is the value that has exactly the same effect as not sending the option. With an MTU of 576 and a 20-octet IP header, the Maximum Datagram Data Size is 556, and subtracting a 20-octet TCP header gives the default MSS of 536.

The MSS option is defined as the maximum number of data octets that may be received by the sender of the option, in segments with no TCP header options, carried in IP datagrams with no IP header options. If headers are larger while the maximum datagram stays 576, the MSS must be reduced. For example, with the IP Security option (11 octets) in use, TCP should send an MSS of 525 (536-11).
sections.plainLanguage: If nobody says anything, everybody assumes the standard box size. If you add extra stickers on the box, you have to say the box holds a bit less.
